newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia All Ordinaries survey-table and comments.
newsitem.headline: Australia All Ordinaries survey-table and comments.

text.p: Reuters Australia conducted a poll of Australian equity strategists and economists last week on their forecasts for the All Ordinaries Index.
The All Ordinaries was up 18.6 points at a record high of 2,692 near the close on Thursday, but the forecasts were made when the index was around 2,640.
A table of their forecasts, the median and mean follow.
Some of the analysts comments also follow.

SNAPSHOT OF ANALYSTS COMMENTS:
PHIL GRAHAM, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ SECURITIES:

"Over the next six months we have industrials going backwards a bit and resources being the driver, but the year after that it is basically reversed, that is, it will be driven from the industrials side."
SHANE OLIVER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, AMP SOCIETY:

"The major driver will be profit growth. You could argue P/E's are a bit stretched at the moment but as profit growth comes through then you should see them come back. I think there are already some signs that profits have stopped falling after the last couple of years as companies start to get their costs back under control. I think as the economy recovers and costs remain under control you should see a profit rebound in industrial profits, and stronger global growth is likely to bring higher commodity prices and therefore higher resource sector profits."
JOHN BANOS, STRATEGIST, MERRILL LYNCH AUSTRALIA:

"The outlook for the economy is very good, the outlook for earnings is improving and Australia has built up a reputation as a low risk market within Asia. But these positives are largely already in valuations. The prospective PE on the industrial market is now 14.3 times May 1998 earnings, which equals the high reached in October 1987. So a lot of the good news on earnings the economy and low risk status relative to Asia is already in the price. In the short-term one of the things that could get the market a bit higher is the possibility of another rate cut, but we wouldn't like to see the market much higher than current levels in the next year or so, that would push it to expensive levels."
PETER MCMANUS, EQUITY STRATEGIST, FIRST PACIFIC STOCKBROKING:

"We see it rising further on the recovery in earnings growth forecasts on the back of the easier monetary policy through the year. A large part of these earnings rises have been factored in, but there's still a fair amount of its left to be put in. But by 1998 bond yields will be heading north and that's going to put a reasonable amount of pressure on the equity markets."
MARCUS TUCK, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HSBC JAMES CAPEL:

"The valuations are still reasonably attractive for our market -- not like in the U.S. We've got an economy that bottomed in the March quarter and we'll have a pick-up through the year and that will help a volumes driven earnings recovery. With inflation staying low and interest rates low and given the valuations remain ok, there's room for the market go further yet."
MARK FULTON, EQUITY STRATEGIST, COUNTY NATWEST AUSTRALIA:
"In the short run resources and in the long run industrials. The low inflation environment, a pick-up in economic growth, which in turn will increase earnings."
HELEN CAMERON, HEAD OF RESEARCH, BNP EQUITIES:

"I think as long as interest rates continue to fall then this market is going up as lower interest rates means a lower cost of capital, which increases cash flow and that starts filtering through to share prices. It is all interest rate driven. Current price earnings ratios are about 19.5 times. In the 1960s it was between 16 to 17 times."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
